report:
Conclusion: I would not answer “yes” for fracture prevention. Whole-body vibration (WBV) is best viewed as unproven for preventing osteoporotic fractures, though it may modestly improve bone mineral density (BMD) and possibly reduce falls in some groups.

Evidence: RCTs and meta-analyses show small, protocol-dependent BMD gains—especially with high-frequency, low-magnitude, higher cumulative dose regimens—but BMD is a surrogate outcome and trials are short, small, and heterogeneous (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y). A broader meta-analysis found WBV might lower fracture risk mainly by reducing falls, not by demonstrating a direct anti-fracture effect (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342). Major guidelines emphasize proven fracture-risk reduction with pharmacologic therapy, calcium/vitamin D adequacy, weight-bearing exercise, and fall prevention; WBV is not a core recommended anti-fracture treatment (https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/osteoporosis-in-postmenopausal-women; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12417299/).

Bottom line: WBV may be an adjunct for selected patients who tolerate it, but it should not replace established osteoporosis care. People with severe osteoporosis, recent fractures, spinal fixation, joint replacements, balance disorders, or pregnancy should seek clinician guidance before using vibration platforms.
